headline: Midnight on the Outgoing: Bass in the Cut, Bunker Getting Hammered on Both Tides
subhead: With the moon waning and the bunker still stacked, the smart money is fishing dark and fishing the ebb — here's where and why.
body_markdown:
Eleven-thirty last night I'm parked on the rocks at the east jetty, rod tip twitching in the dark, and I make the call I make most nights this time of year: I'm not fishing the incoming. I'm waiting for the outgoing to get some current under it, and I'm not casting until the tide's got teeth. That's the whole game right now at Shinnecock Inlet — patience, darkness, and current that means business.

Here's why. Surface water's pushed into the mid-70s across the bay and the inside of the inlet, and that's shoved the bass onto the nocturnal program same as everywhere else on the South Shore. Daytime, you might mark them deep on the drop-off by the Coast Guard station, but they're not eating much until the sun's off the water. So I've been showing up around 10 PM, rigging up on the jetty rocks or working the boat along the rip on the ocean side, and waiting for that outgoing current to really start ripping through the cut — usually a good hour to hour and a half after the tide turns at the bridge.

The pattern's been consistent: bass stacking in the deep hole just inside the inlet, the one that drops to 18-20 feet off the north side, using the current edge as a conveyor belt for whatever bait's getting flushed out of the bay. I've been throwing 2-ounce bucktails with a white or chartreuse curl-tail trailer, casting up-current and letting it swing down through the hole on a tight line, bouncing bottom the whole way. Eels have worked too — a 10-inch live eel drifted through that same seam on an outgoing tide after midnight has been my most consistent producer for fish in the 28-34 inch range, with a few better ones mixed in that I couldn't get a tape on before they let go.

Don't sleep on the jetty rocks themselves on a hard outgoing — bass will sit right in the wash where the current pushes around the rock pile, and a big paddle-tail swimbait worked slow through that foam has fooled some quality fish close enough to see them.

Now, the loud story in this zone right now is bluefish, and I flagged this one myself last week — said the bunker blitz would stay the dominant surf and inlet story until the bait dispersed or the wind broke it up, and that's exactly what's happening. Bunker schools are getting worked over hard right at the inlet mouth and along Tiana Beach, and the blues are chopping through them on both tide stages, not just the outgoing. If you want fast, aggressive action, that's daytime fishing — bring a metal, a Deadly Dick or an Ava jig, and cast into the nervous water where the bunker are getting pushed to the surface. It's not subtle. Blues to 8-10 pounds, sometimes bigger, and they'll cut a bucktail trailer to ribbons if you're not using wire.

Fluke has been the steady, unglamorous program it always is in late July. The flats out toward the middle of the bay, off Cormorant Point and along the edges of the channel toward the canal, are holding shorts in good numbers but the keepers want depth and current. I've had better luck working the deeper edges of the main channel on a stronger tide stage — incoming has been slightly better than outgoing for fluke specifically, which is the opposite of my bass program, so I'll sometimes split a session: fluke on the last of the incoming in daylight, then switch gears and wait for dark for the bass turn. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom in 15-20 feet, have been the ticket, with a squid strip added for scent when the bite's been finicky.

Weakfish at Ponquogue Bridge have been spotty — a few nice ones in the 4-6 pound class coming off the pilings on the outgoing at night, fished with a bucktail-and-bait combo or a bounced bunker chunk, but it's not the every-night thing it can be some Julys. I'd call it a bonus fish right now, not a target species you build a whole trip around. Worth a stop on your way out to the inlet if the tide's right, but don't expect fireworks.

Looking ahead, I don't see much changing in the next few days — the warm water's parked, the bunker aren't going anywhere fast, and that means bluefish stay the headline act while the bass keep working the dark hours. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it's been, I'd keep doing exactly what I'm doing: fishing the outgoing after 10 PM at the inlet, working the deep hole and the jetty wash with eels and bucktails, and using daylight hours for fluke on the bay flats when the tide's pushing hard. If a front comes through and breaks up that bunker concentration, watch for the blues to scatter and possibly push the bass into more predictable feeding windows at dawn — that's when I'd adjust and start fishing first light instead of last light. For now, though, the night owns this inlet, and I'm not changing my clock for anybody.
